title: Migrating to and from Claude
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to plan a controlled migration to or from Claude by documenting an existing integration, isolating provider-specific behavior, and validating observable results before release.
objectives: Document the observable contract of an existing integration before changing providers.
Separate provider-specific translation from provider-neutral application behavior.
Build representative acceptance cases and use them to evaluate a migration.
Classify migration differences and make an evidence-based release or rollback decision.

sections.title: Scope and level
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand basic application inputs, outputs, testing, and error handling. It does not assume knowledge of a particular programming language, library, version, or configuration format.

After completing the module, you can turn an informal provider switch into a controlled migration plan with a documented baseline, an isolated translation boundary, representative acceptance cases, and an explicit release decision.

sections.title: Source correction
paragraphs: The previous source record cited content/modules/anthropic-claude-practice/migrating-to-and-from-claude.json. That citation was an unregistered local publisher path and had never been verified. It has been replaced with Anthropic's official migration guide at the HTTPS address listed in the sources field.

This change affects the citation destination, publisher attribution, and verification record. It does not assert that Claude behavior changed. Whether any wording in the unavailable prior file differed is UNKNOWN, so no unsupported claim about such wording is included.
sections.callout: The correction establishes an official source for the migration guidance. Exact field mappings, version-specific behavior, and configuration keys are omitted because the supplied material does not establish them.

sections.title: Capture the existing contract
paragraphs: Begin by recording what the current integration accepts and what the surrounding application expects it to return. Include representative inputs, required output characteristics, error behavior that the application handles, and operational limits that determine whether a result is acceptable.

Preserve representative examples before changing the provider boundary. Include ordinary cases, difficult cases, and invalid inputs. For each case, write an observable acceptance condition. An acceptance condition should describe what a reviewer or test can inspect rather than relying on a vague judgment such as works well.
Treat the baseline as a behavioral contract, not as a demand that two providers produce identical wording. A migration succeeds when the new path satisfies the application's documented requirements.

sections.title: Isolate provider-specific translation
paragraphs: Place provider-specific request and response translation at a clear boundary. Keep application intent, validation rules, and business decisions outside that boundary. This structure makes it possible to change how the provider is contacted without spreading provider assumptions throughout the application.

For a migration to Claude, translate the application's provider-neutral request into the form required by the Claude integration, then translate the result back into the application's internal form. For a migration away from Claude, apply the same pattern in the opposite direction.
Do not assume that reversing a previous mapping will reproduce the same behavior. Record each translation decision and validate it against the behavioral contract.

sections.title: Evaluate differences systematically
paragraphs: Run the same representative cases through the baseline path and the candidate path. Save enough evidence to compare each result with its acceptance condition. Review failures individually rather than treating every textual difference as a defect.

Classify each important difference as acceptable variation, a translation defect, an application assumption that should be removed, or a blocking mismatch with the contract. Update the translation boundary or the documented requirement only when evidence justifies the change.
Repeat the cases after each correction. Add a new case when an investigation exposes a previously undocumented requirement. This converts discoveries made during migration into regression protection.

sections.title: Make a controlled release decision
paragraphs: Define release criteria before switching production behavior. A useful decision record identifies which acceptance cases passed, which differences were accepted, which risks remain, and who approved the decision.

Keep the previous path available until the candidate path has met the release criteria appropriate to the application. If a blocking mismatch appears, use the documented evidence to correct the translation or restore the previous path rather than improvising under pressure.
A migration is complete when the chosen path satisfies the documented contract and the application no longer depends unintentionally on assumptions from the previous provider.

questions.prompt: What should be documented before changing the provider boundary?
choices: Only the preferred wording of one successful response
The existing integration's observable inputs, expected results, handled errors, and acceptance conditions
An assumed reverse mapping between providers
questions.explanation: The module instructs learners to capture the existing observable contract and representative acceptance conditions before making the change.

questions.prompt: Why should provider-specific translation be placed at a clear boundary?
choices: To isolate provider assumptions from application intent, validation, and business decisions
To guarantee that different providers produce identical wording
To remove the need for acceptance testing
To make every application component aware of the provider
questions.explanation: A clear translation boundary prevents provider assumptions from spreading through the application and makes later changes easier to validate.

questions.prompt: How should a textual difference between the baseline and candidate results be handled?
choices: Treat every difference as a blocking defect
Ignore every difference because providers are different
Compare it with the documented acceptance condition and classify it
questions.explanation: The module says to evaluate observable results against acceptance conditions and classify important differences rather than assuming every variation is a defect.

choices: It established that Claude behavior changed
It added an unsupported version-specific field mapping
It replaced an unverified local source path with Anthropic's official migration guide and updated the verification record
It removed the need for a behavioral baseline
